title: Event driven AI: queues in front of models
story:
The work is slow, the hardware is expensive, and it cannot be scaled up quickly. Meanwhile the traffic arrives in bursts that bear no relation to the capacity you happen to have. A queue between those two facts is the whole design.

What it buys is decoupling. Arrival rate no longer has to equal service rate, so a burst is absorbed rather than refused, and the expensive hardware stays saturated instead of alternating between overwhelmed and idle — which matters more here than in ordinary systems, because utilisation is the entire economic argument for the hardware.

It also composes with the thing that actually determines throughput. High throughput serving requires batching many requests at a time, and the batch size is limited by the per-request cache memory, which is huge and grows and shrinks dynamically and is significantly wasted by fragmentation when managed inefficiently. A queue is where a batch comes from. Without one you batch whatever happened to arrive in the same instant, which is usually one thing; with one you can wait briefly and assemble a full batch, which is the difference between paying for the hardware and using it.

The arithmetic you inherit is Little's. In a queuing process, with one over lambda the mean time between arrivals, L the mean number in the system and W the mean time a unit spends in it, L equals lambda times W — and the relationship is not influenced by the arrival distribution, the service distribution, the service order, or practically anything else. So backlog is arrival rate times waiting time, and a growing queue is a rate mismatch rather than a busy system, which no amount of queue capacity addresses.

Three consequences specific to putting models behind one. The caller receives an acknowledgement rather than an answer, so results have to arrive some other way — a callback, a subscription, a status endpoint — and that is real work you did not have when the answer was inline. Messages can be delivered more than once, so the handler must be idempotent, which for a model call means deciding whether a duplicate re-runs inference or returns the stored result, and inference is expensive enough that the answer should usually be the latter. And failures need somewhere to go, because a message that cannot be processed and is retried forever occupies a worker that costs more per hour than anything else in your system.

problem.name: Buffered model invocation
problem.shape: Expensive slow-to-scale hardware must serve traffic that arrives in bursts unrelated to its capacity.
tell: accelerators alternate between overwhelmed and idle
requests time out during bursts while capacity sits unused minutes later
batches are size one because nothing waits to accumulate
a failed message is retried indefinitely on expensive hardware
problem.move: Put a queue between arrival and service so bursts are absorbed and batches can be assembled, then return an acknowledgement and deliver the result separately. Make the handler idempotent so a redelivery returns the stored result rather than re-running inference, and route repeated failures away from the workers.
problem.invariant: The mean number of items in the system equals arrival rate multiplied by mean time in system, independently of the arrival distribution, the service distribution and the service order.
problem.breaks: A queue absorbs bursts and cannot absorb a sustained rate mismatch, and here the mismatch is harder to fix than usual — service rate is bounded by hardware that takes minutes to acquire, so the backlog grows for the entire duration of the scale-up you started when you noticed.

cost.time: a deliberate wait while a batch assembles, paid by every request in it, which is the price of the utilisation
cost.space: the backlog, plus stored results so a redelivery need not re-run inference
cost.beats: synchronous invocation, which fails during bursts and idles between them, and more replicas, which raises the ceiling without decoupling anything

worked.problem: What does a queue in front of a model buy that more replicas do not?
worked.reasoning:
Decoupling and batch assembly. More replicas raise the ceiling; a queue changes the relationship between arrival and service, and only the second addresses burstiness.

Take the replicas case first, to be fair to it. If your sustained arrival rate genuinely exceeds what current capacity can serve, replicas are the answer and a queue is not — a queue would simply accumulate. So the two are not substitutes, and the question is which problem you have.

What replicas do not fix is burstiness. Traffic arriving unevenly against fixed capacity means that during a peak, requests fail or time out, and minutes later that same capacity sits idle. Adding replicas sized for the peak means paying for peak capacity permanently, which on this hardware is the dominant cost — and it is the cost the whole design exists to avoid. A queue lets the peak wait for capacity that already exists rather than requiring capacity that matches the peak.

The second thing, and the one specific to models, is that a queue is where a batch comes from. Throughput here depends on batching, because high throughput serving requires batching many requests at a time, with the batch size limited by per-request cache memory that is huge and grows and shrinks dynamically and is significantly wasted by fragmentation when managed inefficiently. Without a queue you batch whatever arrived in the same instant, which is usually one request. With one you can wait briefly and assemble a full batch. That difference is the difference between paying for the hardware and using it, and no number of replicas produces it — ten replicas each running batch size one is ten times the cost of one replica running batch size ten.

The arithmetic to bring is Little's: items in the system equals arrival rate times time in system, independently of arrival distribution, service distribution and service order. So the queue depth tells you the rate mismatch directly, and a growing depth is not busyness that will resolve — catching up requires service to exceed arrivals, which the queue does not cause.

The three costs I would name as part of the answer, because they are the actual work. The caller gets an acknowledgement rather than an answer, so results need a delivery path that did not exist before. Redelivery is possible, so the handler must be idempotent — and for inference specifically that should mean returning the stored result rather than re-running, because re-running is expensive enough to matter. And repeated failures need a destination, since a poisoned message retried forever occupies a worker that costs more per hour than anything else you own.

And the limit: the queue absorbs bursts, not a sustained mismatch — and here the mismatch is harder to fix than usual, because service rate is bounded by hardware that takes minutes to acquire, so the backlog grows throughout the scale-up you started when you noticed.

problem.practice: Measure your current batch size distribution. If most batches are size one, you are paying for hardware you are not using, and a short deliberate wait is worth more than another replica. Then check what your handler does on a redelivered message — whether it re-runs inference or returns a stored result.

beats.broke: The work is slow, expensive and served by hardware that cannot be scaled up quickly, while the traffic that wants it arrives in bursts bearing no relation to the capacity you have.
beats.fix: Put a queue in front, so arrival rate is decoupled from service rate, bursts are absorbed rather than refused, and the expensive hardware stays saturated instead of alternating between overwhelmed and idle.
beats.cost: The caller receives an acknowledgement rather than an answer, and any sustained mismatch between arrival and service becomes a backlog whose depth is the arrival rate multiplied by the waiting time.

To be fair to replicas: if the sustained arrival rate genuinely exceeds capacity, replicas are the answer and a queue would simply accumulate. They are not substitutes, so the question is which problem you have.

Uneven traffic against fixed capacity means requests fail during a peak while the same capacity idles minutes later, and sizing replicas for the peak means paying for peak capacity permanently — which on this hardware is the dominant cost and the thing the design exists to avoid. The model-specific point is that a queue is where a batch comes from. The arithmetic to bring is that items in the system equal arrival rate times time in system, independently of the distributions and the service order, so depth reports the rate mismatch directly and a growing queue is not busyness that resolves.
